solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Belch, perhaps, from bishop in play (4)

indicatorNotes.in: the bishop's letter goes inside the word for play

blocks.note: B = bishop, as in chess notation

annotation.surface: A bishop in a stage play lets out an unseemly belch.
annotation.walkthrough: Sir Toby Belch is the drunken uncle in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, so 'Belch, perhaps' defines TOBY by example; 'Belch' only looks like a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Toby is the first name of Sir Toby Belch, so Belch is one bearer of it.

entries.clue: Italian flower in wood losing mass (5)

indicatorNotes.losing: the wood word gives up its M

annotation.surface: An Italian bloom somehow grows in a wood that is shrinking.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'flower' in crosswords is often something that flows: a river. The Tiber runs through Rome.
annotation.definitionFit: The Tiber is a river of Italy, and a river is a flower in the sense of something that flows.

entries.clue: Petty officer: “lawless AB I was not” (9)

indicatorNotes.lawless: letters without rules to keep them in order

annotation.surface: A petty officer protests that the able seaman was not lawless.
annotation.walkthrough: AB (able seaman) belongs to the naval scene, so it reads as a person rather than two letters of fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A boatswain is the ship's officer in charge of rigging and deck crew, a petty officer rank.

entries.clue: Poet Auden abridged Orwell G defends? (10)

indicatorNotes.abridged: Auden is cut short by its last letter
indicatorNotes.defends: the Orwell letters surround and protect the shortened Auden

blocks.note: George Orwell's real name was Eric Blair, so Orwell, G. becomes Blair, E.

annotation.surface: One poet, Auden, is somehow shielded by Orwell.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Orwell G' is written like a surname and initial; swap in the writer's real name and initial and you get Blair E. Charles Baudelaire was the French poet of Les Fleurs du mal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: Charles Baudelaire, author of Les Fleurs du mal, is one of France's great 19th-century poets.

entries.clue: Pilots advanced through rocky heights (8)

blocks.note: A = advanced, as in A level
tors are rocky hilltops, as on Dartmoor

annotation.surface: Pilots have flown on through a range of rocky peaks.
annotation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky outcrop on a hill, a word common in the moorland of south-west England.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an aviator is anyone who flies an aircraft, the older and grander word for a pilot.

entries.clue: Fish on river reserving name for reindeer (6)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue the fish sits above the river
indicatorNotes.reserving: the fish-and-river string keeps the name inside it

blocks.note: a dace is a small freshwater fish

annotation.surface: A fish sits on a riverbank, keeping a name ready for a reindeer.
annotation.walkthrough: Dancer is one of Santa's reindeer in 'The Night Before Christmas'. The N goes into DACE before the R is added.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Santa's sleigh team in 'The Night Before Christmas' includes a reindeer of this name, alongside Dasher and Prancer.

entries.clue: Delay surfacing? Force in sound prepare to attack (3,2,4)

indicatorNotes.in sound: the word for force is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: a lie-in is staying in bed late, putting off getting up
weight is a force; WAIT is said the same way

annotation.surface: Sleeping late is framed as a stalling tactic before an assault.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Surfacing' means getting out of bed, so a delay in surfacing is a lie-in. Weight is a force in the physics sense.
annotation.definitionFit: To lie in wait is to stay hidden ready to ambush.

entries.clue: Sweet preparation here in Paris no good (5)

annotation.surface: A sweet being made here in Paris turns out a failure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' tells you to give the French word, a common crossword signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Icing is a sugary coating prepared for cakes.

entries.clue: Flirt with host (9)

blocks.note: to flirt with an idea is to toy with it, considering it without commitment
a verb here: to host guests at a party

annotation.surface: Someone flirts with the person throwing the party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flirt with' here means consider lightly, as in flirting with an idea, not romance; 'host' is a verb, not the person the surface suggests. To entertain covers both.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one verb: idly weighing a notion you may drop, and receiving guests and giving them a good time.

entries.clue: MacCool, for one, in loud hostelry (4)

annotation.surface: The legendary MacCool turns up in a noisy pub.
annotation.walkthrough: Finn MacCool is the giant-hero of Irish legend, so 'for one' marks him as one Finn among many.
annotation.definitionFit: Finn is the first name of Finn MacCool, the Irish mythic hero.

entries.clue: Very naughty boy welcomes Elizabeth back from Rio? (9)

indicatorNotes.welcomes: the boy's name takes Elizabeth in
indicatorNotes.back: Elizabeth's short form is written backwards

blocks.note: from Monty Python's Life of Brian: 'He's not the Messiah, he's a very naughty boy!'

annotation.surface: A badly behaved boy gives a warm return welcome to Elizabeth, home from Rio.
annotation.walkthrough: The very naughty boy is Brian from Monty Python's Life of Brian. The question mark flags that Rio is one example of where a Brazilian comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: Rio de Janeiro is one city whose natives share this nationality.

entries.clue: Writer George retired to French island (5)

indicatorNotes.retired: withdrawn, so the letters go backwards

annotation.surface: A novelist gives up work and moves to an island off France.
annotation.walkthrough: TO + ILE makes TOILE, which read backwards gives ELIOT. George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, author of Middlemarch.
annotation.definitionFit: George Eliot was the Victorian novelist who wrote Middlemarch.

entries.clue: Sulphur found in check for tree exudation (5)

indicatorNotes.found in: the sulphur symbol sits inside the check word

blocks.note: S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

annotation.surface: A chemist looks for sulphur when testing sap from a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Check' reads as an inspection but means restrain, as a rein does a horse.
annotation.definitionFit: Resin is the sticky substance that oozes from trees.

entries.clue: Little Nell’s introduction in great novel as child (9)

indicatorNotes.introduction: only the first letter of Nell is used
indicatorNotes.in: the little-plus-N string goes inside the rearranged letters
indicatorNotes.novel: new, so the letters of great are made new

blocks.note: anagram fodder, rearranged to T…AGER around WEEN

annotation.surface: Little Nell first appears in a great novel as a child: The Old Curiosity Shop.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Little Nell' is a single Dickens character on the surface, but 'Little' splits off to give WEE. 'Novel' is the anagram signal, not a book.
annotation.definitionFit: A tweenager is a child between about 10 and 12, not quite a teenager.

entries.clue: City pro drawn in by supporter with double D? (8)

indicatorNotes.drawn in by: the pro word is pulled inside the two Ds
indicatorNotes.double: to double something is to make two of it, so the D is written twice

blocks.note: doubling the letter D produces two of them, with FOR drawn in between

annotation.surface: A professional is signed up by a fan, and the question mark winks at a bra size.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' and 'double D' look like football, but together they point to a bra. Bradford is a city in West Yorkshire, England.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: the answer is a former wool town in West Yorkshire with city status since 1897.

entries.clue: Spellbound male in renovated WC with bidet (9)

indicatorNotes.in: the male goes inside the rearranged letters
indicatorNotes.renovated: done up again, so the letters are remade

annotation.surface: A man stands entranced in a refurbished bathroom with toilet and bidet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the two parts of the fodder. WC (water closet) is a toilet.
annotation.definitionFit: To be bewitched is to be spellbound, literally under a spell.

entries.clue: Typhoon perhaps engulfing sappers in ship (9)

indicatorNotes.engulfing: the plane word swallows the sappers

blocks.note: the Eurofighter Typhoon is a fighter jet
RE = Royal Engineers, the British Army's sappers

annotation.surface: A typhoon at sea swallows army engineers aboard a vessel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Typhoon' reads as a storm, which fits a ship, but it is the RAF's Typhoon fighter jet. Sappers are military engineers; in Britain they are the Royal Engineers, RE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: a vessel built to carry freight, that is cargo, is one kind of ship.

entries.clue: Lacking time quick agents dash (6)

indicatorNotes.Lacking: the quick word goes without its T

blocks.note: the CIA is the US intelligence agency

annotation.surface: Short of time, fast-moving spies make a run for it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dash' is a noun, the dashboard; fascia is the British word for a car's dashboard.
annotation.definitionFit: In Britain a car's fascia is its dashboard, or dash.

entries.clue: A piercing yell preceding award for actor (4,5)

indicatorNotes.piercing: what pierces something passes into it, so the A is pushed inside the yell
indicatorNotes.preceding: the yell comes before the award

blocks.note: a grant is an award of money

annotation.surface: A shriek rings out before an acting prize is handed over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Piercing' suits a yell on the surface, but it is the container instruction. Award reads as a trophy for an actor, yet it is a grant.
annotation.definitionFit: Cary Grant was a Hollywood film star of North by Northwest.

entries.clue: Spooner’s not wrapped cheese for martial artist? (5,3)

indicatorNotes.Spooner’s: Rev. Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two words trade their starts

blocks.note: not wrapped = loose; it hands its opening L over and takes BR in exchange
brie is a soft French cheese; it gives up its BR and takes the L back

annotation.surface: An unwrapped cheese is served up for a kung fu fighter.
annotation.walkthrough: Brie is a soft French cheese, and loose means not wrapped. Bruce Lee was the kung fu film star.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the Hong Kong-American star of Enter the Dragon was the best-known kung fu fighter on film.

entries.clue: See 24
Book about Romeo taken in later for monks (8)

indicatorNotes.taken in: Romeo's letter is held inside the later word

blocks.note: Romeo is R in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A book about Romeo gets taken on later by an order of monks.
annotation.walkthrough: Romeo is the radio code word for R, not Shakespeare's lover.
annotation.definitionFit: Monks in an order are called brethren, brothers of the community.

entries.clue: Machine outsiders in Imitation Game deciphered? (6)

indicatorNotes.outsiders: only the first and last letters of Imitation
indicatorNotes.deciphered: decoded, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: first and last letters of Imitation
carried as written into the fodder

annotation.surface: A cipher machine's secrets are cracked in the film The Imitation Game.
annotation.walkthrough: The Imitation Game is the film about Alan Turing breaking the German Enigma cipher, so the whole surface points at the answer. 'In' is the phrase 'outsiders in', not a container.
annotation.definitionFit: Enigma was the German cipher machine of the Second World War.

entries.clue: Projecting well out of the box? (9)

annotation.definition: Projecting well out of the box?

blocks.note: surface: jutting out a long way; meant: coming across well, as a performer projects
surface: beyond a container, or unconventional; meant: from the box, British slang for television

annotation.surface: Something throws its image well beyond the confines of a box.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The box' is British slang for television, and 'out of the box' is also a phrase for unconventional. Someone telegenic projects well from the TV screen.
annotation.definitionFit: Telegenic means looking and coming across well on television.

entries.clue: Student and alumnus near waiting room (5)

blocks.note: L = learner, from the L-plates of learner drivers
OB = old boy, a former pupil
by = near, as in stand by me

annotation.surface: A student and a former pupil hover near the waiting room.
annotation.walkthrough: An old boy is a former pupil of a British school, abbreviated OB.
annotation.definitionFit: A lobby is an entrance hall where visitors wait.

entries.clue: Neoliberal real moaner evicts husband (5-6)

indicatorNotes.evicts: the moaner word throws its H out

blocks.note: right = real, as in a right mess

annotation.surface: A free-market politician grumbles about a husband until he leaves.
annotation.walkthrough: A whinger is a British word for a persistent complainer. 'Real' is used in the sense of a thorough-going, a right one. The answer runs on into 19 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A neoliberal favours free markets, a position on the political right.

entries.clue: Flightless bird‘s tail discussed (4)

indicatorNotes.discussed: talked about, so the word is heard rather than seen

blocks.note: rear = tail, the back end; British speech drops its final R

annotation.surface: People talk about the tail of a bird that cannot fly.
annotation.walkthrough: The match relies on a British accent, which drops the final R of rear. A rhea is a large South American bird like an ostrich.
annotation.definitionFit: The rhea is a large flightless bird of South America.

entries.clue: Effectiveness climate ethics embodies (5)

indicatorNotes.embodies: the phrase contains the answer in its body

annotation.surface: Real effectiveness is what the ethics of climate policy should contain.
annotation.walkthrough: Teeth in the sense of real force, as when a law is said to have teeth.
annotation.definitionFit: A rule with teeth is one with power to be effective.

entries.clue: Hospital with rather loose garment (5)

blocks.note: a bit = rather, as in a bit tired

annotation.surface: A hospital patient wears a rather baggy gown.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rather' modifies 'loose' in the surface, but it is a separate piece meaning a bit.
annotation.definitionFit: A habit is the loose robe worn by a monk or nun.

entries.clue: Joke about bygone English era of prosperity (6,3)

indicatorNotes.about: the joke wraps around the bygone word

blocks.note: olden = bygone, as in olden days

annotation.surface: A wisecrack about the good old days of English prosperity.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bygone English' reads as one phrase, but English stands apart and is added after the container.
annotation.definitionFit: A golden age is a period of peak prosperity or achievement.

entries.clue: Fantasist armed and ready to move (10)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters; 'and' joins the two words

annotation.surface: A dreamer imagines being armed and ready to move into action.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Armed and ready to move' sounds like troops poised to advance, the opposite of an idle dreamer.
annotation.definitionFit: A daydreamer is someone lost in fantasies.

entries.clue: Long throw sees opener dismissed (4)

indicatorNotes.opener dismissed: the first letter is sent away, as a batsman is

annotation.surface: A cricket match where a long throw gets the opening batsman out.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is cricket, where the opener is the first batsman and dismissed means out. 'Long' is the verb, to yearn, not an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to yearn or crave, as in itching to get started.
